hook: You know God didn’t give us a spirit of fear. But did you know Paul wrote it in chains, to a young friend whose tears he remembered?
story:
The man who wrote these words was in chains, and most of his friends were gone.

In this letter Paul calls himself the Lord’s “prisoner”. He writes that “all who are in Asia turned away from me”, and near the end he adds that at his first defense in court “no one came to help me, but all left me.” One visitor stands out. Onesiphorus came to Rome, “sought me diligently and found me”, and “was not ashamed of my chain”.

From there Paul writes to Timothy. He had met him years before in the town of Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother who believed and a Greek father. Since then Timothy had gone with him on his journeys, and Paul had once written of him, “I have no one else like-minded”. Now Paul remembers that Timothy wept, and he has not forgotten it. He writes that he is “longing to see you, remembering your tears, that I may be filled with joy”.

He reminds Timothy of the faith that “lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice”, and of the day Paul laid his hands on him. Then come the words so many people now know by heart: “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.”

Paul does not write you. He writes us. The man in chains counts himself in.

moment:
Why would Paul need to say this to Timothy? The letters to him give a few clues, and they are human ones. Timothy was young enough that Paul once told him, “Let no man despise your youth”. He had “frequent infirmities” of the stomach. Years earlier, sending him to the church in Corinth, Paul had asked the believers there, “see that he is with you without fear”. And Timothy had been left behind at Ephesus with a hard task: to “command certain men not to teach a different doctrine”.

Now his teacher is in prison and expects to die. Later in the letter Paul says it plainly: “the time of my departure has come.” He asks for the cloak he left at Troas, and for his books. Twice he asks Timothy to come quickly, the second time with a deadline: “Be diligent to come before winter.”

So this verse was not written into a calm life. A man facing death writes it to a younger friend who has much that could frighten him: standing alone, being linked to a prisoner, suffering the same. In the very next line Paul says what he is asking for: “don’t be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner”.
around:
The verse is the hinge of the chapter. Before it, Paul remembers: tears, a grandmother and a mother, hands laid on a young man. After it, he asks Timothy to “endure hardship for the Good News according to the power of God”, and he gives his own example: “Yet I am not ashamed, for I know him whom I have believed”. He ends the chapter with two kinds of people: those in Asia who turned away, and Onesiphorus, who came looking.

The word Paul uses for fear here is found nowhere else in the New Testament. It is not the common Greek word for being afraid, which can be good or bad. This one, deilia, is always used in a bad sense: timidity, cowardice, a shrinking back. The last word of the verse, translated self-control, also appears only here.

Since the early nineteenth century many scholars have held that a later follower of Paul wrote this letter in his name. Others still defend that Paul wrote it himself. The letter presents these words as Paul’s, written in chains.
after:
The letter ends with a request: “Be diligent to come before winter.” The Bible never tells us whether Timothy made it in time.

It does tell us that at some point Timothy too was held. The letter to the Hebrews, whose writer is not named, closes with the news: “Know that our brother Timothy has been freed”.

About Paul, the church historian Eusebius passed on that he wrote this letter during his last imprisonment in Rome, the one in which he died, and that it is recorded that Paul was beheaded in Rome during the persecution under Nero.

Eusebius also records that Timothy was the first to lead the church in Ephesus as its bishop. A later tradition, retold in the old Catholic Encyclopedia, says that Timothy never married, led that church until he was over eighty, and was then beaten to death by pagans. That is tradition, not the Bible. If it is right, the young man who was told not to shrink back stayed with his church into old age.

The words outlived them both. In the same letter Paul had asked Timothy to pass on what he had heard to “faithful men who will be able to teach others also.” This verse is one of the things that was passed on.
readings:
Many readers turn to this verse when they are anxious, and hear in it that fear does not have to rule a life that belongs to God. Read in its chapter, the fear Paul means is also more specific: the shrinking back that would make Timothy ashamed of the Good News and of his friend in prison. The answer Paul gives is not only a calmer feeling but a courage that acts: to testify, to visit, to endure hardship. Both readings hold the same promise of what God gives, one for the inner life and one for the life lived in front of others.

Readers have also weighed the word spirit. The World English Bible writes it with a small letter here. John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter, heard in it the Holy Spirit whom believers receive, and a few lines later Paul speaks of “the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.”

The last word has been read in more than one way as well. The World English Bible says self-control. Greek dictionaries also give soundness of mind, discipline, and even a calling of someone back to good sense. Chrysostom offered several meanings at once: a healthy state of the soul, a sober mind, or a mind sobered by the troubles that come.
point: Quoted on its own, this verse can sound like a promise that a believer will never feel afraid. In its chapter it is something stronger. It was written by a man in chains, whom almost everyone had left, to a young friend who had wept. Paul does not deny the danger. He names what God has given instead of fear: power, love, and self-control, enough to stand by the Good News and by a friend in prison. And he points to a man who did exactly that: Onesiphorus, who searched Rome for him and was not ashamed of his chain.
lesson:
This verse was not written to someone with nothing to fear, and it does not ask you to pretend you have nothing to fear either.

Paul was in chains, and Timothy had wept. Paul does not promise his friend that the danger will pass. He reminds him of what God has already given, and then he asks him to act on it: not to be ashamed, to keep going, to come.

Maybe fear is making your life smaller right now: fear of what people will think, of standing alone, of what comes next. You do not have to wait until the fear is gone to take one faithful step. Read the whole chapter; it takes a few minutes. You could pray the verse the way Paul wrote it, with us in it, for yourself and for someone you love who is afraid.

And if you do not share this faith, the scene still says something true about people: a friend who is not ashamed of your chain is worth more than a crowd that turns away.

echoes.note: Paul draws the same line in another letter: “you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear”. What God gives makes people children who call him Father, not slaves who cower.
“There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear”. John sets love against fear just as Paul does, and both say that love is what God gives.

Threatened by the council, the believers prayed, were filled with the Holy Spirit, and “spoke the word of God with boldness.” It is the courage Paul asks of Timothy: not to be ashamed of the testimony.
